risk_nodes.l3: Socioeconomic impacts of LLM may be highly disruptive
risk_nodes.definition: The risk that rapid advances in language models disrupt workers' incomes by accelerating job turnover and displacement, including among highly skilled workers, by biasing technological progress against labor so that labor's share of wealth declines, and ultimately, if models and robots can perform virtually all work tasks, by driving wages down toward the marginal cost of machines. Together these dynamics pose fundamental challenges for labor markets and income distribution.

risk_nodes.definition_original: Rapid advances in LLMs pose three distinct sets of challenges for workers’ incomes (Korinek and Stiglitz, 2019; Susskind, 2023). First, they are likely to accelerate the rate of job turnover and disruption —– affecting more workers, including more highly skilled workers, and making the adjustment process for society more difficult than what we were used to from prior technological advances...Second, although technological progress means that society may produce more wealth overall, there is a risk that the general-purpose nature of LLMs may lead to progress that is biased against labor, meaning that the share of that wealth that goes to labor may decline...Third, if future LLMs and robots advance to the point where they can perform virtually all the work tasks, they would disrupt labor markets more fundamentally: if machines can do workers’ jobs, wages would fall would disrupt labor markets more fundamentally: if machines can do workers’ jobs, wages would fall to machines’ user cost (Korinek and Juelfs, 2023). This would pose fundamental challenges for labor markets and income distribution (Korinek, 2023).
risk_nodes.korean_definition: 언어모델의 급속한 발전이 고숙련 노동자까지 포함한 일자리 대체와 이직을 가속하고 기술 진보를 노동에 불리하게 편향시켜 노동분배율을 낮추며 결국 임금을 기계 한계비용 수준으로 끌어내리는 위험으로 정의된다.

risk_nodes.l3: Socioeconomic impacts of LLM may be highly disruptive
risk_nodes.definition: The risk that language models worsen socioeconomic inequality, depending on how the gains from the technology are distributed. Inequality may rise if returns shift from labor to capital, if the high fixed costs and network effects of frontier models produce monopolistic 'algorithmic monoculture' that lets developers extract rents, and if unequal access to productivity-enhancing AI tools disadvantages those excluded for financial, educational, or geopolitical reasons.
risk_nodes.evidence_status: incremental markdown risk source; semantically new L4 node
risk_nodes.definition_original: LLMs could potentially worsen socioeconomic inequalities (Capraro et al., 2023). Effects on inequal- ity are closely linked to the effects of LLMs on workers but ultimately depend on how the fruits of technological progress are distributed...First, if the role and compensation of capital rise and the role and compensation of labor decline in an LLM-powered economy, inequality may go up because work is the main source of income for the majority of people...Second, the large fixed cost of training cutting-edge LLMs and the network effects involved imply that the market for the most advanced LLMs tends towards a natural monopoly structure in which only one or a small number of players will be successful, a phenomenon that has been termed ‘algorithmic monoculture’ in the literature (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021; Bommasani et al., 2022). As a result, LLM developers may amass significant market power. This might result in reduced social welfare, and lead to LLM-providers extracting monopoly rents from their customers (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021; Jagadeesan et al., 2023)...Third, as LLMs are becoming more powerful, who has access and who hasn’t is becoming a more and more important question. For example, automated coding tools have been shown to produce significant productivity gains, e.g. > 50% in some cases (Peng et al., 2023). Individuals who don’t have access —– whether it is for financial reasons, for reasons of education, because of corporate or governmental policies, or for geopolitical reasons — might be at a growing disadvantage
risk_nodes.korean_definition: 언어모델의 이익이 노동에서 자본으로 이전되거나, 첨단 모델의 독점적 '알고리즘 단일문화'가 지대를 추출하거나, 접근 격차가 발생하면서 사회경제적 불평등을 악화시키는 위험으로 정의된다.

The workforce of developing countries may suffer from a retrenchment of outsourcing as many simple cognitive tasks that used to be performed in developing countries — for example, in call centers –— can be automated with LLMs. This may adversely affect the economies of the poor countries (Georgieva, 2024).

risk_nodes.l4_label: Corporate power may impeded effective governance
risk_nodes.phrase: corporate power may impeded effective governance
risk_nodes.definition: The risk that the growing power of large corporations developing language models impedes effective governance. The power asymmetry between these firms and civil society raises the danger that AI governance becomes excessively favorable to industry, producing regulatory capture at the expense of other societal groups, particularly marginalized communities historically harmed by poorly designed AI.
risk_nodes.evidence_status: incremental markdown risk source; semantically new L4 node
risk_nodes.definition_original: The increasing power and influence of large corporations may make effective governance difficult. There exists a power asymmetry between corporate entities profiting from LLMs and other social groups (e.g. civil society). State-of-the-art LLMs are developed by or in partnership with, some of the world’s largest private tech companies...This poses a risk of governance protocols related to LLMs becoming excessively favorable to tech companies, potentially leading to regulatory capture at the cost of the interests of other societal groups, particularly marginalized communities who have historically been disproportionately affected by poorly designed AI technologies (Reventlow, 2021).
risk_nodes.korean_definition: 언어모델을 개발하는 대기업의 권력이 커지면서 시민사회와의 권력 비대칭으로 AI 거버넌스가 산업에 지나치게 유리해지고 규제 포획이 일어나 소외 공동체에 피해를 주는 위험으로 정의된다.

risk_nodes.l2: AI system security vulnerabilities and attacks
risk_nodes.l4_label: Jailbreaks and prompt injections threaten security of LLMs
risk_nodes.phrase: jailbreaks and prompt injections threaten security of llms
risk_nodes.definition: The risk that language models are not adversarially robust and remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and prompt-injection attacks. The lack of standardized evaluation and efficient white-box robustness methods, the new attack avenues opened by additional modalities, and the absence of robust privilege levels within model inputs together make these attacks particularly difficult to eliminate.
risk_nodes.evidence_status: incremental markdown risk source; semantically new L4 node
risk_nodes.definition_original: LLMs are not adversarially robust and are vulnerable to security failures such as jailbreaks and prompt-injection attacks. While a number of jailbreak attacks have been proposed in the literature, the lack of standardized evaluation makes it difficult to compare them. We also do not have efficient white-box methods to evaluate adver- sarial robustness. Multi-modal LLMs may further allow novel types of jailbreaks via additional modalities. Finally, the lack of robust privilege levels within the LLM input means that jailbreaking and prompt-injection attacks may be particularly hard to eliminate altogether.
risk_nodes.korean_definition: 언어 모델이 적대적으로 견고하지 못해 탈옥과 프롬프트 인젝션 공격에 취약하며, 표준 평가와 효율적 화이트박스 견고성 기법의 부재 및 모달리티 확장이 이를 제거하기 어렵게 만드는 위험으로 정의된다.

risk_nodes.definition: The risk that adversaries perturb a model's training data to implant backdoors, hidden vulnerabilities that can later be triggered at inference time. This is especially challenging for large language models because they are trained on data scraped from untrusted sources such as the internet, which adversaries can readily poison.
risk_nodes.evidence_status: incremental markdown risk source; semantically new L4 node
risk_nodes.definition_original: The previous section explored jailbreaks and other forms of adversarial prompts as ways to elicit harmful capabilities acquired during pretraining. These methods make no assumptions about the training data. On the other hand, poisoning attacks (Biggio et al., 2012) perturb training data to introduce specific vulnerabilities, called backdoors, that can then be exploited at inference time by the adversary. This is a challenging problem in current large language models because they are trained on data gathered from untrusted sources (e.g. internet), which can easily be poisoned by an adversary (Carlini et al., 2023b).

risk_nodes.definition_original: As the general capabilities of LLM-empowered systems improve, the negative consequences and risks induced by these systems also get increasingly alarming accordingly, especially in high-stakes areas [28, 146]. [171] reveal the existence of the moral direction with the sentence embeddings of moral questions. However, the distribution of the pre-training corpora may not match exactly with that of the human society [56] and pieces of knowledge are not guaranteed to be equally learned. As a result, value mismatches may occur.

risk_metadata.design: framework-derived initial L4 risk overlay anchored to the existing STPI topic space
risk_metadata.evidence_linking: Each L4 risk node carries a representative evidence_url. Specific papers are used when available; otherwise the node links to the defining source framework or report.
risk_metadata.integration_note: Uploaded MIT AI Risk Repository leaf risks were filtered, embedded, semantically de-duplicated, hierarchically mapped, and anchored to the existing STPI/Risk map.
risk_metadata.physical_ai_risk_overlay_design: duplicate-tolerant L1 overlay for AI systems that perceive, reason, and act in the physical world
risk_metadata.latest_incremental_source: Physical AI benchmark and survey sources
risk_metadata.latest_incremental_duplicate_policy: Exact source IDs and semantic duplicates update existing node metadata; only genuinely new leaf risks are added.
risk_metadata.risk_impact_scoring: Risk node radius is proportional to severity x probability proxy; AIID severity/frequency are used when observed and missing values are imputed with L2/L1/global partial pooling.
risk_metadata.latest_physical_ai_benchmark_integration: Benchmark-specific Physical AI risks were integrated as L4 nodes; exact or high-similarity duplicates update existing node evidence.
risk_metadata.l3_refined: redundant L3 re-derived via embedding sub-clustering + c-TF-IDF

latest_pluralistic_value_misalignment_up.method: candidate L4 risk phrases were matched to OpenAlex/arXiv evidence and retained only when the direct evidence URL opened with HTTP 2xx/3xx.

latest_governance_accountability_update.method: Governance/accountability L4 candidates were matched to OpenAlex and local AI-risk paper pools and retained only when a direct evidence URL opened with HTTP 2xx/3xx.

korean_policy_risk_evidence_update.matching_rule: domestic Korean AI policy reports with Korean risk cues were embedded with BGE-M3 and matched to L4 risk cards by cosine similarity

taxonomy_card_deduplication.method: Conservative within-branch merge using punctuation, quote, hyphen, and simple singular-plural label normalization.
